newsitem.title: USA: CBOE plan to halve S&P 100 met with skepticism.
newsitem.headline: CBOE plan to halve S&P 100 met with skepticism.

text.p: The Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) is considering cutting the size of its S&P 100 stock index in half to attract more retail investors, but many market participants are skeptical of the plan.

Traders, brokers and analysts said Wednesday that such a move would not likely provide the liquidity boost which the exchange appears to be seeking because the index is inherently an institutional product.

"There's a real problem with liquidity," said Jerry Hegarty, an analyst at Thomson Financial Services. "Yesterday, for example, there were 90,000 (OEX) puts and 50,000 calls traded for a total of 140,000," he explained. "That is just too thin for bigger traders to be getting off 100 and 200 lots."
He said cutting the index in half might boost volume briefly but would not be a longer-term fix for low liquidity.

"Even at the Merc (Chicago Mercantile Exchange) and Board of Trade (Chicago Board of Trade), most retail clients are not actually out trading these products themselves," one SPX and OEX broker said. "They're letting professional money do it."

Thomas Ascher, CBOE vice chairman, said the exchange is performing "due diligence" with its members and the industry to gauge broad sentiment on the issue before moving ahead with a halving of the OEX.

"We are considering splitting the OEX and as part of that process we are engaging in due diligence," he said in an interview. "The committee that oversees OEX procedure has been considering this and had a discussion" Tuesday.
Exchange sources said the committee decided to consider an OEX split at a later date rather than endorsing the idea outright.
The OEX closed Wednesday at 778.52, down 7.37 points.
Cutting the index in half would lower the prices of put and call options on the index and theoretically attract smaller investors, analysts said.

But with individual equity options volume climbing dramatically, some in the industry do not see the need to tinker with what is the CBOE's most successful product and the world's most active index option.
"Don't fix something that's not broken" said Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co and head of the Committee on Options, an industry group.
OEX volume in 1996 declined by 21.1 percent, but individual equity volume rose by 14.8 percent.

"There's enough interest (in the OEX) now that I don't think it will be spurred on by the fact that it is lower," the head of an options desk in New York said. "I don't think it will really gather any more interest."
But some participants favor halving the OEX.
"They should do it," said Jay Shartsis, head of options trading at R.F. Lafferty & Co in New York. "Ten points isn't what it once was and the spreads are wider. I think it's frightening people away."
